**Our Jenkins CI reporter is causing the flood. GitHub is delivering notifications for the comments it posts.** I found an exact match for your examples.

One personal CI run—**build #147**, testing commit [`3e6a051`](https://github.com/gkeyllorg/gkeyll/commit/3e6a0519acb8396e8c650ed4f0a5bd8790351305#commitcomment-204308347)—created **122 separate GitHub comments in about two minutes**. It published roughly **7 MB of report text**, containing 16,874 warnings, with 16,179 also listed under “New warnings vs c8e4e…”. Many are repeated simulation warnings about very small time steps.

The [reporting script](/var/home/mrosen/gkeyll/ci/jenkins/github_report.py:393) splits large reports into roughly 60 KB chunks and publishes **every chunk as a separate comment**, without a limit on the number of comments. That produces “CI diagnostics (continued)” and “All warnings … (part 3).” I also found the [exact “All warnings (216) (part 3)” comment](https://github.com/gkeyllorg/gkeyll/commit/e22d1629d00804a64b2a8cb05ddea0d07bb1f090#commitcomment-204332035).

People watching the repository or subscribed to the relevant conversation can receive email notifications for that activity, depending on their [GitHub notification settings](https://docs.github.com/en/subscriptions-and-notifications/concepts/about-notifications). The 122-comment burst explains the thread containing around 100 emails; I haven’t inspected anyone’s mailbox to establish the exact delivery count.

**The fix belongs in our reporter:** publish one bounded summary with warning counts and a few examples, and keep the full diagnostics in a linked report/artifact. Repeated time-step warnings should also be grouped. Changing everyone’s email preferences would only hide the underlying problem.

I’ll check GitHub’s options for keeping complete CI reports and downloadable files accessible while avoiding a separate notification for every report section.

content.text:
**Yes—we can keep every detail on GitHub while eliminating the flood of comment emails.** The change is to store the report as files and link to it from the CI result. The amount of information can remain exactly the same.

For Gkeyll, I recommend this arrangement:

1. **Publish complete reports to a dedicated GitHub repository**, such as `gkeyllorg/ci-reports`. Each run gets a directory identified by tested commit, machine, and build number.
2. **Provide a rendered Markdown index** linking to test results, timings, all warnings, all errors, and logs. Large sections can span linked Markdown files, preserving the current collapsible sections.
3. **Point the existing CI “Details” button directly to that index.** GitHub’s commit-status API already supports a report URL, so the entry point stays on the tested commit/PR. [GitHub status documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/commits/statuses)
4. **Stop posting diagnostic continuation comments.** We could retain one short completion comment, or use the status alone and create no report comments.

That turns the 122-comment run into **one report publication and zero or one comments**, with all 16,874 warnings still accessible. File publication doesn’t create those comment notifications; other notifications still depend on subscriptions and repository configuration.

There are several file-storage options:

| Option | Reading experience | Main tradeoff |
|---|---|---|
| **Files in a dedicated reports repository** | Read formatted Markdown directly on `github.com`; browse or download logs | Accumulated reports grow Git history |
| **GitHub Pages** | Browse a complete HTML report with navigation, search, and collapsible sections | GitHub-hosted, but outside the `github.com` interface; published sites have a 1 GB limit |
| **Release assets** | Download complete reports and compressed log bundles | Primarily downloads rather than browser-rendered reports |
| **Actions artifacts** | Download files associated with an Actions run | Requires a publishing workflow, signed-in access, and retention management; default expiration is 90 days |

GitHub documents [repository file uploads](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/repos/contents), [Pages limits](https://docs.github.com/en/pages/getting-started-with-github-pages/github-pages-limits), [release-asset uploads](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/releases/assets), and [artifact access and retention](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/manage-workflow-runs/download-workflow-artifacts).

**My preference is the dedicated reports repository for browser-readable reports, with compressed bulk logs as release assets if storage growth warrants it.** Jenkins can upload those assets through GitHub’s supported API. We should avoid publishing a new release for every build, since that introduces another notification source.

This preserves inspection entirely through GitHub, requires no Jenkins access for readers, and lets us keep the existing green/red status interface. The main design decision is how long to retain historical reports as storage grows.

Would putting this inside github checks resolve this issue? Maybe for now we can just report the total number of warnings, new warnings, compress the timestep warnings, and keep  this code for later if we put this in github checks. Can Jenkins post actions artifacts?

I’ll verify the limits of GitHub Checks and artifact uploads from Jenkins, then inspect how to show warning counts and group repeated time-step warnings while preserving the full report for later use.

GitHub Checks would remove the stream of comment notifications, but its report fields have size limits, and a Jenkins-created check does not come with Actions artifact storage. Jenkins can trigger an Actions workflow to fetch and upload its files; it cannot upload Actions artifacts directly with its existing GitHub token.

I’m applying the testing-and-verification skill for the interim change: warning counts and grouped time-step warnings in the posted report, with the full diagnostic output retained as a Jenkins artifact. Other large sections can still produce continuation comments, so this reduces the flood without guaranteeing one email per run.

The reporter now shows the total warning count and new-warning messages, grouping repeated time-step warnings by test/log and threshold. It retains every warning and its context in `ci-report-warnings.md`.

All 49 focused reporting tests passed. A fixture with 17,000 time-step warnings produces one comment page while preserving every message in the artifact.

Implemented locally in the [reporter](/var/home/mrosen/gkeyll/ci/jenkins/github_report.py):

- GitHub shows **total warning count and new-warning messages**.
- Repeated time-step warnings are grouped by test/log, with counts and time-step ranges.
- Complete warning details remain in the Jenkins artifact `ci-report-warnings.md`. The full formatter is preserved for future use.

**All 49 reporting tests passed.** A 17,000-time-step-warning fixture now fits on one comment page. Other unusually large report sections can still produce continuation comments. This takes effect when Jenkins loads the updated reporting code.

On your earlier questions:

**GitHub Checks:** Yes, replacing comments with check output would eliminate this comment-notification flood. Checks have output-size limits, so complete large logs would still need linked files. [Checks documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/checks/runs)

**Jenkins uploading Actions artifacts:** Not directly using its ordinary GitHub token—the supported artifact REST API has no upload endpoint. Jenkins can trigger an Actions workflow that retrieves the files and uploads them using `actions/upload-artifact`. That requires a file-transfer route accessible to the workflow; creating a check alone does not provide artifact storage. [Artifact API](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/actions/artifacts)
